lessons.title: States of matter

slides.title: What is matter?
slides.oldHtml:
What is matter?

Anything that has mass and volume
Mass: the amount of matter (kg)
Volume: the space it takes up (m3 or L)
Solid
Liquid
Gas
slides.newHtml:
What is matter?

Anything that has mass and volume
Mass: the amount of matter (kg)
Volume: the space it takes up (m3 or L)
Solid
Liquid
Gas

slides.title: Solids
slides.oldHtml:
Solids

  • Fixed positions in a regular lattice
  • Vibrate about fixed positions (more when heated)
  • Fixed shape and fixed volume
  • High density — cannot be compressed
Forces of attraction: Strong
slides.newHtml:
Solids

  • Fixed positions in a regular lattice
  • Vibrate about fixed positions (more when heated)
  • Fixed shape and fixed volume
  • High density — cannot be compressed
Forces of attraction: Strong

slides.title: Liquids
slides.oldHtml:
Liquids

  • Close together (touching), random arrangement
  • Move past each other (faster when heated)
  • Fixed volume, takes the shape of the container
  • Cannot be compressed easily
Forces of attraction: Weak
slides.newHtml:
Liquids

  • Close together (touching), random arrangement
  • Move past each other (faster when heated)
  • Fixed volume, takes the shape of the container
  • Cannot be compressed easily
Forces of attraction: Weak

slides.title: Gases
slides.oldHtml:
Gases

  • Random and far apart
  • Move freely in all directions (faster when heated)
  • No fixed shape or volume — fill any container
  • Low density — easily compressed
Forces of attraction: Very weak
slides.newHtml:
Gases

  • Random and far apart
  • Move freely in all directions (faster when heated)
  • No fixed shape or volume — fill any container

Forces of attraction: Very weak

slides.title: Changes of state
slides.oldHtml:
Changes of state

Caused by changes in temperature and/or pressure
  • Change the particles' kinetic energy
  • They are reversible physical changes
  • Also called interconversions or transitions
Dry ice (solid CO₂) sublimating into gas
slides.newHtml:
Changes of state

Reversible physical changes caused by changing temperature or pressure (also called interconversions)
Dry ice sublimating

slides.title: Evaporation
slides.oldHtml:
Evaporation

Liquid → gas without boiling
  • Fastest particles at the surface escape into the air
  • Happens at any temperature below the boiling point
  • Faster at higher temperature, wind, or wider surface
Boiling forms gas bubbles throughout the whole liquid at the boiling point.
slides.newHtml:
Evaporation

Liquid → gas without boiling
  • Fastest particles escape from the surface
  • Happens at any temperature below the boiling point
  • Boiling forms bubbles throughout the liquid at the boiling point

slides.title: Temperature and state
slides.oldHtml:
Temperature and state

Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C
What state is water at 24 °C?
→ Liquid (24 °C is between 0 °C and 100 °C)
  • At exactly 0 °C or 100 °C, it can be in either state
  • Compare the given temperature to the melting and boiling points
slides.newHtml:
Temperature and state

Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.
What state is it at 24 °C?
  • Liquid — 24 °C is between 0 °C and 100 °C
  • Below 0 °C → solid; above 100 °C → gas
  • At exactly 0 °C or 100 °C, it can be in either state

slides.title: Which has stronger forces?
slides.oldHtml:
Which has stronger forces?

Air or olive oil?
  • Air is a gas at room temperature (boils at about −195 °C)
  • Olive oil is a liquid at room temperature (boiling point well above 25 °C)
Stronger forces → more energy needed to separate particles → higher boiling point
slides.newHtml:
Which has stronger forces?

At room temperature (25 °C), air is a gas and olive oil is a liquid.

slides.title: Forces and boiling point
slides.newHtml:
Forces and boiling point

Weak forces (e.g. air)
Little energy needed to separate → low boiling point
Stronger forces (e.g. olive oil)
More energy needed to separate → higher boiling point
Stronger forces of attraction → more energy needed → higher boiling point

slides.title: Particles are fast!
slides.oldHtml:
Particles are fast!

Gas particles travel at hundreds of m/s (hydrogen ≈ 1700 m/s)
So why is diffusion slow?
  • Particles constantly collide and change direction
  • Higher temperature → faster particles → faster diffusion

lessons.title: Ionic bonding

slides.title: Molecules can be ions too
slides.oldHtml:
Molecules can be ions too

Hydroxide, OH−: an oxygen atom joined to a hydrogen atom
The group has gained one extra electron
→ charge of 1−
also: NO3−,  CO32−,  SO42−,  NH4+

slides.title: Electron transfer
slides.oldHtml:
Electron transfer

The metal (Na) loses an electron → cation Na+  |  the non-metal (F) gains it → anion F−
slides.newHtml:
Electron transfer

The metal (Na) loses an electron → cation Na+
The non-metal (F) gains it → anion F−
